```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
```

Genre labels are a classification that films do not respect. A film is
rarely only a drama or only a comedy; it is a romantic comedy, a crime drama,
an animated adventure. The combinations that recur describe the conventions
of film production better than any single label does, and the way they change
over time traces the history of those conventions. A co-occurrence network
makes the combinations visible: each genre is a node, and two genres are
linked by the films they share.

The difficulty is that raw counts of shared films are dominated by the most
common genres. A genre that appears in most films co-occurs with everything,
so its links say more about its frequency than about any affinity with a
partner. Similarity measures correct for this by comparing the number of
shared films with the number each genre would share by chance or with the
size of the smaller genre (van Eck & Waltman, 2009). This case study builds
the genre network of 1,000 IMDb films, asks which genres go together once
frequency is taken into account, how the network is organized, and whether
the combinations differ across decades and between the highest-rated films
and the rest.

```{r package}
library(cooccure)
```

## Data

`movies` is a sample of 1,000 films from the IMDb non-commercial datasets,
released between 1970 and 2024, each with an IMDb rating of at least 7.0 and
at least 1,000 votes. The roles of its columns in this analysis are:

- **Transaction:** a film, identified by `tconst` and named by
  `primaryTitle`.
- **Items:** the genres in `genres`, separated by commas.
- **Grouping variables:** the release `decade`, and the IMDb rating
  `averageRating`, from which a rating band is derived.
- **Not used:** `startYear` and `numVotes`.

```{r data}
head(movies)
```

A film carries up to three genres. A film with a single genre contributes an
item but no pair, so the number of genres per film bounds what the network
can show.

```{r genres-per-film}
with(movies, table(genres_per_film = lengths(strsplit(genres, ","))))
```

Of the 1,000 films, 231 have one genre, 300 have two and 469 have three, so
769 films contribute at least one pair.

## Which genres appear together most often?

The first network uses raw counts: the weight of an edge is the number of
films tagged with both genres.

```{r raw}
raw_genres <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",")
print(raw_genres, n = 8)
```

The 22 genres form 129 pairs out of 231 possible, a density of 0.558. Drama
is involved in six of the eight heaviest pairs, beginning with 159 films that
are both comedy and drama and 131 that are both drama and romance. The node
table shows why.

```{r raw-nodes}
head(as.data.frame(raw_genres, what = "nodes"), 8)
```

Drama appears in 634 of the 1,000 films (`frequency`) and is linked to 20 of
the other 21 genres (`degree`). A genre this common will head any list of
raw counts, whatever its affinity with its partners, so the raw network
answers how often pairs occur rather than which genres belong together.

## Which genres belong together once frequency is accounted for?

The Jaccard index divides the number of shared films by the number of films
that carry either genre, so a pair scores high only when the two genres
rarely appear apart.

```{r jaccard}
jaccard_genres <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                               similarity = "jaccard")
print(jaccard_genres, n = 8)
```

The ranking changes. Adventure and Animation lead with a Jaccard index of
0.285 although they share only 39 films, and Action and Crime come second.
Comedy and Drama, the heaviest raw pair, falls to third (0.211): the two
genres share many films, but each also appears in many films without the
other.

Association strength goes further. It divides the shared films by the
product of the two genres' frequencies, which is proportional to the number
of shared films expected if genres were assigned independently. Rare genres
can reach high association from a single film, so genres in fewer than 20
films are removed first.

```{r association}
association_genres <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                                   similarity = "association",
                                   min_occur = 20)
print(association_genres, n = 8)
```

Five genres fall below 20 films, leaving 17 genres and 998 films; the two
films lost carried only rare genres. Drama has disappeared from the top of
the list. The pairs that co-occur most above chance are Adventure and
Animation, History and War, Mystery and Thriller, Documentary and Music, and
Animation with Fantasy and with Family: combinations that define a kind of
film, such as the animated family adventure, the war history, or the music
documentary. Several of these rest on few films (History and War on 9), so
their weights describe a strong tendency within a small set.

## How is the genre network organized?

The Jaccard network restricted to genres in at least 20 films is drawn with
**cograph**, with node size proportional to degree and edge width to the
Jaccard index.

```{r drawing, eval = has_cograph, fig.height = 5.5}
genre_network <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                              similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 20,
                              output = "cograph")
cograph::splot(genre_network, layout = "fr", seed = 1,
               scale_nodes_by = "degree", node_fill = "#56B4E9",
               edge_color = "#999999", label_size = 0.8)
```

In the drawing the heaviest edges are the widest, so the pairs from the
Jaccard table above (Adventure and Animation, Action and Crime, Comedy and
Drama) stand out against a mesh of thin edges: 17 genres share 102 of the
136 possible links.

The degree distribution of the full Jaccard network summarizes how evenly
the links are spread.

```{r degree}
plot(jaccard_genres, type = "degree")
```

The genres with the fewest links are at the end of the node table.

```{r degree-tail}
tail(as.data.frame(jaccard_genres, what = "nodes"), 5)
```

Apart from Drama (20 links) and Comedy (19), 16 of the 22 genres are linked to
between 9 and 17 of the other 21. Sport and Musical have 7 links, and only
News (2) and Western (1), each tagged on a single film, are nearly isolated.
The network is dense rather than organized around a few hubs, so what
distinguishes one genre from another is the weight of its links, not their
number.

## Have genre combinations changed across decades?

`split_by` builds one network per decade with the same settings. Genres in
fewer than five films of a decade are removed so that each decade's network
is not driven by single films.

```{r decades}
decade_genres <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                              split_by = "decade", similarity = "jaccard",
                              min_occur = 5)
as.data.frame(decade_genres, what = "groups")
```

The decades differ in size, from 12 genres in the 1970s to 17 in the 2010s,
the decade with the most films in the sample. The density of the network
rises from 0.473 in the 1980s to 0.625 in the 2010s, so more genre
combinations occur, and the mean Jaccard index falls from 0.1334 in the
1970s to 0.0666 in the 2010s, so each combination is less exclusive. The three
strongest pairs of each decade show which combinations persisted.

```{r decade-top}
decade_top <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                           split_by = "decade", similarity = "jaccard",
                           min_occur = 5, top_n = 3)
print(decade_top, n = 18)
```

Adventure and Animation is among the three strongest pairs in four of the
six decades (1970s, 1990s, 2010s and 2020s), and Action and Crime in three
(1980s, 2000s and 2010s). Comedy and Drama enters the top three only in the
1990s and 2000s, and Documentary and Music in the 1980s and 2020s. The
animated adventure is the most stable combination in the sample.

## Do the highest-rated films combine genres differently?

A rating band separates films rated 8 or higher from those rated 7 to 7.9,
and one network is built per band.

```{r bands}
rated <- transform(movies, rating_band = ifelse(averageRating >= 8,
                                                "8 and above", "7 to 7.9"))
with(rated, table(rating_band))
```

The top band holds 139 films and the lower band 861, so genres are required
to appear in at least 10 films of a band.

```{r band-top}
cooccurrence(rated, field = "genres", sep = ",", split_by = "rating_band",
             similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 10, top_n = 4)
```

The lower band repeats the pattern of the whole sample: Adventure and
Animation, Action and Crime, Comedy and Drama. Among the films rated 8 or
higher, Documentary and Music is the strongest pair (0.333, ten films),
followed by Comedy and Drama, Biography and Documentary, and Comedy and
Romance; Action and Adventure pairs do not reach the top four. The top band
is small, and its strongest pairs rest on 6 to 19 films, so the difference
indicates where highly rated films concentrate rather than an established
contrast.

## Summary

Raw counts of genre pairs reflect how common each genre is, with Drama at
the top of almost every list. Normalized by the Jaccard index or by
association strength, the network shows the combinations that define kinds
of film: animated adventures, crime thrillers, war histories, music
documentaries. The network is dense rather than clustered, its combinations
became more numerous and less exclusive from the 1970s to the 2010s, and the
highest-rated films lean toward documentary and biography pairs. For the
choice of measure see the [guide to similarity measures](similarity-measures.html),
and for per-group networks the [guide to comparing groups](comparing-groups.html).
The same films are the source of the
[actor collaboration case study](case-actor-collaboration.html).

## References

van Eck, N. J., & Waltman, L. (2009). How to normalize cooccurrence data? An
analysis of some well-known similarity measures. *Journal of the American
Society for Information Science and Technology*, 60(8), 1635–1651.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.21075>
